text: Now what is more foolish than refusing to learn, simply because one has not been learning for a long time?
plain: Not having learned in the past is no reason to stay ignorant now.

text: Wisdom comes haphazard to no man.
plain: Nobody drifts into wisdom. You go get it.

text: Money will come of its own accord; titles will be given to you; influence and authority will perhaps be thrust upon you; but virtue will not fall upon you by chance.
plain: Money, titles and influence can land on you by luck. Character never does.

text: A dwarf is not tall, though he stand upon a mountain-top; a colossal statue will still be tall, though you place it in a well.
plain: Status does not make a man big and lowliness does not make him small.

text: If an evil has been pondered beforehand, the blow is gentle when it comes.
plain: Think through the bad outcome ahead of time and it hits softer.

text: To the fool, however, and to him who trusts in fortune, each event as it arrives “comes in a new and sudden form,” and a large part of evil, to the inexperienced, consists in its novelty.
plain: Much of what hurts is that it is new. Expect trouble and half the sting is gone.

text: We sometimes hear the inexperienced say: “I knew that this was in store for me.” But the wise man knows that all things are in store for him. Whatever happens, he says: “I knew it.”
plain: The wise man is never surprised, because he already counted on everything.

text: At whatever point you leave off living, provided you leave off nobly, your life is a whole.
plain: A life is complete if it is lived honorably, however long it runs.

text: It is not an important matter to live; all your slaves live, and so do all animals; but it is important to die honourably, sensibly, bravely.
plain: Staying alive is nothing special. Doing it, and dying, with courage is.

text: Reflect how long you have been doing the same thing: food, sleep, lust,—this is one’s daily round.
plain: Eat, sleep, repeat. Look at how little your days differ.

text: Would you not think him an utter fool who wept because he was not alive a thousand years ago? And is he not just as much of a fool who weeps because he will not be alive a thousand years from now?
plain: Grieving that you were not born earlier is as silly as grieving that you will not live later.

text: No journey but has its end.
plain: Everything you are travelling toward ends.

text: You wish to live; well, do you know how to live? You are afraid to die. But come now: is this life of yours anything but death?
plain: Wanting more life is cheap. Are you actually living the one you have?

text: There is no life that is not short.
plain: Every life is short. Stop measuring it against longer ones.

text: It is with life as it is with a play,—it matters not how long the action is spun out, but how good the acting is.
plain: Length is not the point. How well you play it is.

text: Nothing, my excellent Lucilius, refreshes and aids a sick man so much as the affection of his friends; nothing so steals away the expectation and the fear of death.
plain: Nothing heals a sick man like the people who love him.

text: There is no sorrow in the world, when we have escaped from the fear of death.
plain: Lose the fear of dying and most of your sorrows have nothing to hold onto.

text: You will die, not because you are ill, but because you are alive; even when you have been cured, the same end awaits you; when you have recovered, it will be not death, but ill-health, that you have escaped.
plain: You die because you are alive. Getting well only delays it.

text: No man can suffer both severely and for a long time; Nature, who loves us most tenderly, has so constituted us as to make pain either endurable or short.
plain: Pain is either bearable or brief. It cannot be both unbearable and endless.

text: Everything depends on opinion; ambition, luxury, greed, hark back to opinion. It is according to opinion that we suffer. A man is as wretched as he has convinced himself that he is.
plain: Your suffering follows what you tell yourself about it.

text: Pain is slight if opinion has added nothing to it; but if, on the other hand, you begin to encourage yourself and say, “It is nothing,—a trifling matter at most; keep a stout heart and it will soon cease”; then in thinking it slight, you will make it slight.
plain: Do not pile commentary on the pain. Call it small and it shrinks.

text: What benefit is there in reviewing past sufferings, and in being unhappy, just because once you were unhappy?
plain: Replaying old pain just makes you hurt twice.

text: Two elements must therefore be rooted out once for all,—the fear of future suffering, and the recollection of past suffering; since the latter no longer concerns me, and the former concerns me not yet.
plain: The past hurt is over and the future hurt has not come. Drop both.

text: Is it for this purpose that we are strong,—that we may have light burdens to bear?
plain: Strength exists to carry heavy things. Do not ask for light ones.

text: Be your own spectator; seek your own applause.
plain: Do the hard thing for your own eyes. You are the audience that counts.

text: “A single day among the learned lasts longer than the longest life of the ignorant.”
plain: One day used well outweighs a lifetime wasted.

text: Meanwhile, hold fast to this thought, and grip it close: yield not to adversity; trust not to prosperity; keep before your eyes the full scope of Fortune’s power, as if she would surely do whatever is in her power to do.
plain: Do not fold under hardship or relax in good times. Expect fortune to do her worst.

text: Fame is the shadow of virtue; it will attend virtue even against her will.
plain: Do the work right and recognition follows without you chasing it.

text: How long did men believe Democritus to be mad! Glory barely came to Socrates.
plain: The greats were doubted and ignored while they lived.

text: That man is born merely for a few, who thinks only of the people of his own generation.
plain: Do not build only for the people around you now.

text: Pretence accomplishes nothing. Few are deceived by a mask that is easily drawn over the face. Truth is the same in every part.
plain: Fakes get seen through. Truth holds together everywhere.

text: How many men, I say to myself, train their bodies, and how few train their minds!
plain: Everyone trains the body. Almost nobody trains the mind.

text: All that goes to make you a good man lies within yourself. And what do you need in order to become good? To wish it.
plain: Becoming good costs nothing but wanting it.

text: First of all, free yourself from the fear of death, for death puts the yoke about our necks; then free yourself from the fear of poverty.
plain: Two fears keep people leashed: dying and going broke.

text: If you would know how little evil there is in poverty, compare the faces of the poor with those of the rich; the poor man smiles more often and more genuinely; his troubles do not go deep down; even if any anxiety comes upon him, it passes like a fitful cloud.
plain: Poor people often laugh more. Their worries pass quickly.

text: If you wish to set a value on yourself, put away your money, your estates, your honours, and look into your own soul. At present, you are taking the word of others for what you are.
plain: Strip away money and titles and look at the person. Do not let others set your price.

text: In order to discover one grateful person, it is worth while to make trial of many ungrateful ones.
plain: Most people won't be grateful. Helping a lot of them to find the one who is can still be worth it.

text: After a shipwreck, sailors try the sea again. The banker is not frightened away from the forum by the swindler.
plain: One loss is no reason to quit the sea.

text: My master Attalus used to say: “Evil herself drinks the largest portion of her own poison.”
plain: Doing wrong hurts the wrongdoer most.

text: And what is more wretched than a man who forgets his benefits and clings to his injuries?
plain: Holding grudges while forgetting kindness makes you miserable.

text: We hold nothing dearer than a benefit, so long as we are seeking one; we hold nothing cheaper after we have received it.
plain: We crave favors until we get them, then forget them.

text: We consider not what we have obtained, but what we are to seek.
plain: Greed looks at what is next and ignores what it already has.

text: I hold that he who lies on a perfumed couch is no less dead than he who is dragged along by the executioner’s hook.
plain: A soft life of ease is a slow way of being dead.

text: Leisure without study is death; it is a tomb for the living man.
plain: Rest with no growth in it is a tomb.

text: As if the real causes of our anxieties did not follow us across the seas!
plain: Running away does not work. Your worries travel with you.

text: Fortune has not the long reach with which we credit her; she can seize none except him that clings to her.
plain: Luck can only take what you are gripping. Hold your possessions loosely.

text: It is not pain that we praise, it is the man whom pain has not coerced. One praises not death, but the man whose soul death takes away before it can confound it.
plain: We admire the person who stays steady through hardship, not the hardship.

text: The soul must be hardened by long practice, so that it may learn to endure the sight and the approach of death.
plain: Courage is trained slowly by facing hard things on purpose.

text: When truth is at stake, we must act more frankly; and when fear is to be combated, we must act more bravely.
plain: Speak plainly and meet fear head on.

text: “Fellow-soldiers, let us to our breakfast, knowing that we shall sup in Hades!”
plain: Leonidas told his men to eat well, since they would dine in the underworld.

text: I shall keep watching myself continually, and—a most useful habit—shall review each day.
plain: Audit your own day, every day.

text: Drunkenness kindles and discloses every kind of vice, and removes the sense of shame that veils our evil undertakings.
plain: Drink does not make you worse, it takes away the shame that was holding you back.

text: Do that which is easiest of all—namely, demonstrate that what men call pleasures are punishments as soon as they have exceeded due bounds.
plain: Any pleasure past its limit turns into punishment.

text: Abandon riches, which are either a danger or a burden to the possessor. Abandon the pleasures of the body and of the mind; they only soften and weaken you.
plain: Money is a danger or a burden. Comfort makes you soft.

text: Abandon your quest for office; it is a swollen, idle, and empty thing, a thing that has no goal, as anxious to see no one outstrip it as to see no one at its heels.
plain: Chasing rank is empty, a race with no finish line.

text: Vices are never genuinely tamed.
plain: A bad habit stays wild underneath. Do not trust yourself with it.

text: How have I the power to bring something to a close, when I have not had the power to check it at the beginning? For it is easier to keep a thing out than to keep it under after you have let it in.
plain: Easier to keep a habit out than to master it once it is in.

text: It is proper for him to be careful, but not to be fearful.
plain: Be careful, not afraid.

text: Liberty is lost unless we despise those things which put the yoke upon our necks.
plain: You are free only if you can do without the things that control you.

text: Because of his poverty he is prevented from showing how the State should be handled; but he teaches, none the less, how poverty should be handled.
plain: Being broke does not stop you from showing how to handle it well.

text: Pain, want, disgrace, imprisonment, exile,—these are universally to be feared; but when they encounter the wise man, they are tamed.
plain: The scariest things stop being scary once you can handle them.

text: We old men must learn this precept; for there is none of us who is not planting an olive-yard for his successor.
plain: Plant trees whose shade you will never sit in.

text: We have become so luxurious that we will have nothing but precious stones to walk upon.
plain: Comfort keeps demanding more until nothing is enough.

text: He who blushes at riding in a rattle-trap will boast when he rides in style.
plain: If you feel shame in a beat-up ride, you will brag in a fancy one. Both are about other people's eyes.

text: Neither master nor mule is improved by such trappings.
plain: Nice stuff does not improve the owner.

text: Money tumbles into the hands of certain men as a shilling tumbles down a sewer.
plain: Plenty of rich people got it by luck, not merit.

text: Why, then, is the wise man great? Because he has a great soul.
plain: Greatness is in the soul, not in what you own.

text: Those things which are goods produce confidence, but riches produce shamelessness. The things which are goods give us greatness of soul, but riches give us arrogance. And arrogance is nothing else than a false show of greatness.
plain: Wealth makes people arrogant, which is greatness faked.
